## Summary

A test is tautological or vacuous when nothing it runs can make it red: its expected and actual values share a source (the code under test, the test's own mock, or a constant), no assertion actually executes, an error path is swallowed, or the recorded "expected" value was produced by the code itself. The detectors that have evidence behind them are dynamic, not purely static: assertion counters, extreme-transformation/mutation runs, and "new tests must fail on the base commit" checks — with measured precision, e.g. Google's diff-scoped mutation testing (findings' reported usefulness improved 20%→80% with a not-useful feedback loop) and a 400-merged-PR replay where every one of 31 "moved expectation" flags was a real, intended change.

## Assumptions

- The question is answered for a reviewer agent (quack) that can run deterministic gates over a diff and a local decision model. "Mechanically detectable" therefore means: CI-runnable check (lint, test run, static analysis, mutation run) vs. something a 27B-class model must judge by reading.
- "Asserts constants" is read as: the assertion's checked value is a literal/constant (or the same value on both sides), so no behavior of the code under test can influence the outcome.
- "Fails on the base commit" covers the check the sources describe: run the tests a change *adds* against the base code; each should fail there. A related direction (run *old* tests against new code, flagging moved expectations) is covered separately because the best benchmark evidence is for it.
- Exact false-positive rates are rarely published per indicator; where a source quantifies them I cite it, otherwise I describe the known FP classes and note the gap.

## Findings

### 1. What "tautological/vacuous" means, and why green is not evidence

- A tautological test "cannot fail because the result it checks and the value it expects come from the same source" — the code under test, a mock, or a constant; developers also call them vacuous tests or "tests that test nothing"; the code still counts toward coverage, which "records which lines ran, not which results were checked." [s22]
- The mechanism in four steps: the test gets the actual from the code/mock/constant; gets the expected from that *same* source (not from the written rule, i.e. the test oracle); compares them; so a bug appears on both sides and the assertion passes. A tautological test can still fail on an exception, but on a *wrong answer* it reports a false pass. [s22]
- Real-world instance (aliasing): two variables named differently were the same mutable object, so "a set is considered a subset of itself. The assertion is tautological. It can never fail." The author reports this mistake happens to him "perhaps a few times a month," even to experienced TDD practitioners; the mitigation is that red-green-refactor "encourages you to run each new test and see it fail. If you haven't seen it fail, you don't know if you've avoided a tautology." [s1]
- Practitioner framing a reviewer can use as the core rubric question: "could this test ever fail? ... If you can't describe a plausible code change that would break the test, you haven't written a test." A test that can't fail "can actively launder an existing problem into something that looks resolved." [s5]

### 2. Test asserts its own mock (mocked subject / over-mocking)

- **Definition.** "The test replaces the component it claims to check with a mock, then asserts the value it told the mock to return. A test that mocks a `delivery_fee` function to return 0.00 and then expects 0.00 checks only the mock." [s22] Same as over-mocking: "the mock setup dwarfs the actual verification ... the test is testing the mocks, not the code." [s19]
- **Example.**
  ```js
  vi.mock('./database', () => ({ db: { insert: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ id: '123' }) } }));
  const result = await createOrder({...});
  expect(result.id).toBe('123'); // tests only that the mock returned what we set up
  ```
  [s19] Python version: `repo.find.return_value = User(id=1, name="Ada"); assert svc.get(1).name == "Ada"` — "none of its logic is being checked." [s8]
- **Reviewer's tell (what to cite in the diff).** The assertion's expected value is identical to a value placed in the arrange block: "if you can predict the assertion from the setup alone, the test is checking the double rather than the code, and it will keep passing through any change that leaves the delegation intact." [s8] Concretely: `expect(x).toBe(v)` where `v` is the argument of a `mockResolvedValue/thenReturn/expect(:encode, v)` in the same test; or an assertion written *inside* the body of a mock/fake (so it only runs if the mock is invoked at all). [s8][s12]
- **Detection.** Partially mechanical: matching each assertion's constant to the test's own stubbed values is a dataflow check over the diff (flag, not fail); a full mock of the module under test is flaggable statically (hollowtest "flags ... a mock of the very module under test"). [s7] Decisive check is dynamic: strip the SUT body to a bare delegation and rerun — if green, the test checked the double. [s8] Whether a given stub is *appropriate* (external paid service vs. internal dependency) needs judgement: "Mocking internal application code ... is almost always a sign of poor test design." [s19]
- **False positives.** Moderate and structural: interaction tests legitimately verify call arguments, and hollowtest therefore "reports tests whose only checks are `toBeDefined()` or `toHaveBeenCalled()` as weak, not hollow." [s7] A test that mocks only one boundary of a multi-dependency function is usually fine. [s19]

### 3. Recomputes the expected value with the code under test

- **Definition.** "The test builds its expected value with the code's own function, formula, or constants, so it repeats the code instead of checking it." [s22] Lint-rule formulation: "One side of the assertion computes its value with arithmetic, concatenation, or formatting over values the test holds, so the test can make the same mistake as the code it checks." [s21] Test-smell form: "one does not want to duplicate the logic between tests and code. So replicating a regexp or something else in the test is not an option." [s2]
- **Example.**
  ```py
  def with_tax(subtotal, rate): return subtotal + subtotal * rate
  assert with_tax(80, 0.25) == 80 + 80 * 0.25   # same formula twice
  ```
  [s21] And the constant-import variant: `FREE_DELIVERY_MIN = 250.00` (bug: should be 200.00) with `expected = 0.00 if subtotal >= FREE_DELIVERY_MIN else 15.00` — "no threshold value can make it fail"; fixing is to state the rule's value literally: `assert delivery_fee(200.00) == 0.00`. [s22]
- **Reviewer's tell.** An expected value that "calls the code under test, imports from its module, or comes from a mock the test set up is not independent." [s22] Diff heuristic the author recommends: "treat a diff that replaces a literal expected value with a call or an import as a finding." [s22]
- **Detection.** Lint catches the syntax-only shape (e.g. a linter rule that flags computed expected values, `ur lint --rule circular-expectation`, which suggests "state the expected value as a literal"), but "a linter checks syntax and cannot tell which function is under test, so it does not flag an expected value taken from that function" — most cases need reading the expected value's provenance (judgement) or a mutation run (mechanical). [s21][s22]
- **False positives.** Known and bounded: "a computation over constants alone is a stated value" — `2 * 3` is fine; so is a shared pure helper with independent tests. [s21] The main FP class is legitimate derivation (e.g. table-driven tests that compute expectations from a spec), which is why the rule ships as a *note* level, not a warning. [s21]

### 4. Asserts constants / compares a value with itself

- **Definition.** "Both sides of the assertion are the same term, once each local the test assigns once is replaced by its value, so the assertion cannot fail." [s20] Self-comparison: "The test compares a value or a constant with itself, e.g. `assert total == total`." [s22] Smell form ("Self-Test"): "Tests that do not compare a result with an expected value, but with the result itself." [s16]
- **Example.**
  ```py
  expected = cart.total()
  assert cart.total() == expected      # [s20]
  expect(total).toEqual(total)         # [s7]
  ```
  [s16] shows the same computation over two locally built collections: the expected list is filtered with the same `isEligibleForCountry("PL")` logic as the code under test, so `assertThat(methodsForCountry).isEqualTo(methodsAvailableInPoland)` agrees by construction. [s16]
- **Reviewer's tell.** Syntactic: the assertion's two operands are the same expression, or one is an alias of the other, or both derive from the same local constant. This is the rare tautology provable from the test file alone.
- **Detection.** Mechanical: dedicated lint rules exist — `tautological-assertion` "an assertion compares a value with itself," on by default at warning level, with the hint "compare with a value stated independently of the code"; pylint's comparison-with-itself check "flags `assert total == total`, but not a function call compared with itself or a formula repeated in the test." [s20][s22]
- **False positives.** Low but nonzero and documented: testing a type's own equality operator (`assert_eq!(x, x)` in Rust) is a legitimate test of `==`, and the linter reports it anyway, so "a test of a type's own == ... is reported too; mark one written on purpose with ur-allow." [s20]

### 5. No assertion (and its subtler cousin, the rotten green test)

- **Definition.** "A test that does not contain at least one valid assertion is not a real test as it does only execute plain source-code, but never assert any data, state or functionality." [s3] Distinct from a *rotten green* test: one that passes while "some or all of its assertions are not actually executed" — e.g. an assertion inside a loop that iterates over an empty collection. [s6]
- **Examples.** (a) Shopify: `Minitest::Mock#expect(:encode, v) do |arg| assert_equal(...); assert_equal(...) end` — the block is never run by `expect`, and the run reports "1 runs, **0 assertions**" for a test with two visible asserts. [s4] (b) Real bug hidden in production code: a test in Alibaba Sentinel sleeps, then iterates `leapArray.list()` which is now empty, so `assertTrue(...)` never executes while the test stays green. [s6] (c) Assertion placed *inside* a mocked method body: aws-sdk-java's `prepareSocket` test asserted inside the mock's `setEnabledProtocols` override; "When running an extreme transformation on this method, the assertion is never evaluated and the test cases pass silently" — fixed by moving the assertion out, PR merged. [s12]
- **Reviewer's tell in the diff.** Zero assertion calls in the new test body; an assertion inside a `for`/`if`/`do`-block that depends on data the SUT produces; an assertion inside a test double's method; a loop over a collection that could be empty (fix: assert the collection is non-empty first — "flunk('test requires non-empty published posts collection')"). [s4][s6][s12]
- **Detection.** Mechanical for the plain case: a framework assertion counter — Shopify hooks `after_teardown` and raises if `assertions.zero?` (skipped/erroring tests exempted); in JS, `expect.hasAssertions()` "causes it to fail if no assertions ran." Caveat: "at the moment RSpec does not have an assertions/expectations counter." [s4][s19] The rotten-green case needs a test *run* with call-site instrumentation (static analysis finds assertion call sites and helper methods; the run checks which executed) — the authors' method "does not report false negatives," and in their final validation "we did not find any that was incorrectly labeled as fully rotten (i.e., we did not find any false positives)." Runtime cost: 1–20 minutes per Java project. [s6]
- **False positives.** Real, and the authors classify them: missed-fail (catch block with `assertTrue(false)`), missed-skip (early `return` instead of `assumeTrue`), and context-dependent assertions are "essentially warnings ... rather than serious problems"; genuinely useful no-assertion smoke/build-verification tests exist and should be exempted. [s6][s4] Assertion-count gates therefore need exemptions (s4: wrap "nothing raised" tests in `assert_nothing_raised`), and weak-but-present assertions (`toBeDefined`) should be reported as weak, not hollow. [s7]

### 6. Catches every error

- **Definition.** A `try/catch` that swallows the exception makes the test pass whether or not the code throws: "what happens if `SomeFunction()` doesn't throw an exception? The test still passes. In fact, the test doesn't test anything." [s10]
- **Example.**
  ```csharp
  try { SomeFunction(null); } catch (Exception) { }   // passes with or without the throw
  ```
  [s10] The same shape, found in the wild by extreme transformation: `try { it.add(value); } catch (Exception ex) {}` — "If the method is emptied, then nothing happens and the test passes"; the merged fix adds `fail()` after the call so no-throw is a failure. [s12] And the assertion-inside-catch variant (requests): a timeout test that asserts the message inside `except Timeout` — "if the request stopped timing out, the test would pass." [s7]
- **Reviewer's tell in the diff.** A catch block with no assertion/fail/rethrow; an assertion in a catch with no `fail()` (or equivalent) on the fall-through path; a catch of the base exception type, which "will also catch a base class of the thrown exception" and "can hide subtle changes" (e.g. `ArgumentException` vs `ArgumentNullException`). [s10]
- **Detection.** Mechanical: a static pattern over the diff (catch without fail/rethrow; assert-only-in-catch) is reliably recognizable and is implemented in hollowtest's rule set. [s7] The stronger form — "does this test still pass if the method never throws?" — is a one-line mutation (SBR: remove the `throw`) plus a test run. The recommended refactor is framework-native: `[ExpectedException(typeof(ArgumentNullException))]` "forces one to be specific about the exception; the test will fail even if the thrown exception inherits from the expected exception." [s10]
- **False positives.** The documented legit case: "Even if you want to catch the exception to make assertions about some of its properties ... be sure to rethrow the exception" — catch-assert-rethrow is sound, so a naive "assert in catch" rule flags it; the rethrow presence is the mechanical discriminator. [s10] Also, a test whose whole purpose is "this path throws" is only valid if "not throwing" is a genuine defect for that input (judgement).

### 7. Snapshot: records whatever is produced

- **Definition.** "A snapshot test works the same way [as a tautology], because its first snapshot stores whatever the code produced. A snapshot that is recorded again on every failure, e.g. with the `--updateSnapshot` flag in Jest, checks nothing." But note the nuance: "Snapshot tests are not tautological by design, because a snapshot test fails when later output differs from the saved output. The first snapshot records whatever the code produced, though, so a wrong output becomes the expected value." [s22]
- **Example.** The "it renders" test: "render the component, take a snapshot, and voila! More test coverage. But what is this actually testing? ... That React can call render() properly? I believe the React codebase has that covered." [s15]
- **Reviewer's tell in the diff.** A new test whose only assertion is `toMatchSnapshot()`; a PR that *both* changes the code and the `.snap` file (the snapshot was updated to match, possibly without being read); the ezCater experience: ambiguous diffs made people "not paying attention to the snapshot output, and just updating the snapshot to get tests to pass" — after ~6 months they "removed or replaced nearly every existing snapshot test." [s15]
- **Detection.** Mechanical for the purest cases (test with only a snapshot call; snapshot file auto-updated in the same commit as the code it pins); whether the recorded output is *correct* is definitionally not checkable from the test itself — it requires an independent assertion or a human review of the snapshot hunk. [s22][s15]
- **False positives.** Genuine use exists: "Checking CSS is probably the strongest case for keeping around snapshot tests." [s15] And a reviewed, stable snapshot is a real regression check. [s22] A reviewer should flag *new* first-run snapshots and *touched* snapshots, not every snapshot test.

### 8. Tests the framework instead of the code

- **Definition.** "If you're using a framework you pretty much have to assume it works. Testing it along with your other tests only clutters things up." [s11] For mock-centric suites: "If one uses too many mock objects that interact with each other, the test will only test the interaction between them instead of the functionality of the production code." [s18]
- **Example.** Over-mocked glue code: "The only fact the code contributes is that get() hands back whatever find() returned" — the assertion is verifying that the mock returns its stub, and "strip the body of get() down to a bare call to find() and the test still passes." [s8] The aws-sdk example is the same idea: the assertion sits inside the mocked object, so the test passes by virtue of the mock's own behavior. [s12]
- **Reviewer's tell in the diff.** The class under test is a thin pass-through over doubles and every asserted value originates in arrange; or the test's SUT *is* a mock/fixture (asserting "the mock returns what it was told to return"); or the asserted property is a framework guarantee (e.g. "can React call `render()` properly?"). [s8][s15][s12]
- **Detection.** Mostly judgement: identifying the real SUT and where each asserted value comes from is the hard part, and the smell catalog gives this entry no code example. Partially mechanical proxies: extreme transformation ("strip the SUT body → still green" ⇒ the test is checking the double/framework), and the ratio of mock-arrange lines to production assertions. [s8][s12]
- **False positives.** No quantitative data found. Legitimate cases: verifying an adapter's integration with the framework it targets, and framework-level tests that intentionally live with the framework. The catalog's own framing is a heuristic ("only clutters things up"), so treat as a judgement finding, not a gate. [s11]

### 9. Detection: mutation testing, with evidence

- **Definition.** "Mutation testing assesses test suite efficacy by inserting small faults into programs and measuring the ability of the test suite to detect them. It is widely considered the strongest test criterion in terms of finding the most faults and it subsumes a number of other coverage criteria." [s9]
- **Evidence it works.**
  - *Industrial scale/precision:* Google runs diff-based, probabilistic mutation analysis inside mandatory code review for 6,000 engineers on ~30% of coverage-calculated diffs; dataset: 72,425 diffs, 1,159,723 mutants, 150,854 actionable findings; with a one-click "not useful" feedback loop, "the reported usefulness of the surfaced results improved from 20% to 80%." Baseline noise: median 2 living mutants per diff, 99th percentile 43. Mutating only *covered, diff-touched, non-arid* lines (logging etc.) is what makes it reviewable. [s9]
  - *Correlation with real weakness:* pseudo-tested methods (covered, but no test fails when the body is stripped) exist in **all** 21 Java projects studied (PS_RATE 1%–46%, 2,540 methods total), and "in average the mutation score of required methods is 52% above that of pseudo-tested methods" (Wilcoxon p<0.01, effect size 1.5); extreme case scifio: 1% vs 84% mutants killed. Developers merged fixes for 7 of 8 reported issues. [s12]
  - *Catching the specific anti-patterns in this report:* hollowtest's `--mutate` ("breaks your code on purpose (> becomes >=, && becomes ||)") on 18 well-known repos — most scored in the high 90s, but it surfaced 36 zod assertions written `expect(...).toBeNull;` (missing parens — "when you add the `()`, the v4 tests fail", i.e. the hollow test was hiding a real bug), 53 zod assertions inside catch, swr un-awaited `.resolves` assertions, and requests' timeout test. [s7] Practitioner rule: "If a test suite fails to catch mutations, it's a strong signal that coverage is superficial." [s19]
- **Known limits (i.e. its false-positive/false-negative profile).** (a) "Mutation testing shows where the suite is weak, not which test is at fault" — a surviving mutant "points to code that no test checks, not to one test," and "a sound test on the same line hides a tautological one." [s22] (b) Some "pseudo-tested" mutants are killed trivially by an exception, so MS is never 0% — kills by crash don't equal assertion-based kills. [s12] (c) "Tools differ in which code they mutate, so a constant defined outside a function may get no mutant." (d) "It needs a test run for each mutant" — cost is the binding constraint, which is exactly why the Google system restricts mutants to diff-touched lines; that diff-scoped shape is the practical one for a per-PR reviewer. [s22][s9]

### 10. Detection: "fails on the base commit"

- **Definition.** "A new test that already passes on the old code doesn't test the change." The check (e.g. `goalline prove-red`) "runs the tests a change adds against the base code: each one should fail there. Any that pass are flagged." It's the industrialization of the red step: "Test-driven development starts red: a test for a bug should fail before the fix and pass after it. A coding agent asked to fix a bug and add a test can write a test that passes either way, and CI shows two green checks." [s13] Same advice from the field: "Keep the new unit test, undo the other code changes. The unit test now needs to fail. If your newly introduced unit test still passes, then you didn't expose the bug in the test. A simple check but often neglected." [s14] It is also precisely ploeh's point: "If you haven't seen it fail, you don't know if you've avoided a tautology." [s1]
- **Mechanics (implementable as a gate).** Check out the PR head in a scratch copy, restore all non-test files from `git merge-base` (tests stay at the PR version), run only the new/changed tests, and fail if they pass. A concrete GitHub Action doing exactly this (restore `:^\^tests/` from merge-base, then `if python -m unittest; then exit 1`) is published. [s13][s14]
- **What it catches.** By construction it catches the vacuous forms that pass on base: assertionless tests, mock-tautologies, recomputed expected values, swallowed-error tests, and first-run snapshots — all pass on the base commit and get flagged. [s13][s22]
- **Evidence it works (the related "moved old expectation" check).** A replay of the last 400 merged PRs of pallets/click and pallets/jinja: 126 PRs edited an existing test (a naive "test file changed" alarm would fire on all 126); the check flagged 31, each "with their old and new values," and "every flag was a deliberate change that its PR explains in one line, and 4 changed what users see without the changelog saying so" — i.e., zero spurious flags after fixes, ~3 min of machine time per 200-PR replay. [s17]
- **False positives / limits (documented).** (a) New tests written for behavior that *already existed and was correct* will pass on base and be flagged — the author's answer is scope it to fix PRs and use a label/gate toggle: "You can see the first one failed: The problem is that the old code already passes the new tests. This means the tests don't test the change. The second one passes but only because no new tests were added at all." [s14] (b) Misidentifying which files are tests (jinja's `src/jinja2/tests.py` is production code) caused false flags; fixed by taking the files the runner actually collects. (c) Old tests that fail on their own base code (e.g. Python-version-specific tracebacks) read as "moved expectations"; fixed by also running the failing old test on the old code and counting it only if it passes there. [s17] (d) It cannot flag a tautological test for *unchanged* code; mutation testing is the complement that does. [s22][s12]

### 11. Practical gate stack for a reviewer agent (synthesis)

Cheap static gates over the diff (high precision, low recall): no-assertion call in new test bodies; `expect(x).toBe(x)`-style self-comparisons; catch-without-fail and assert-only-in-catch; test body whose only assertion is `toMatchSnapshot()`; assertion constant identical to a value stubbed in the same test; diff that replaces a literal expected value with a call/import of the module under test. [s20][s7][s10][s22]
Dynamic gates (lower precision, higher recall): assertion counter at teardown (exempt smoke tests and skipped tests); `expect.hasAssertions()`; prove-red (new tests must fail on base, scoped to bugfix PRs); call-site-instrumented runs to find unexecuted assertions (rotten green); diff-scoped mutation on changed production lines with surviving mutants surfaced as findings (accept that a finding means "this line is weakly checked," not "this test is tautological"; keep a not-useful feedback loop, since that is what took Google's finding usefulness from 20% to 80%). [s4][s13][s6][s9][s22]
Judgement (decision model): expected-value provenance vs. the PR's stated requirement; whether a stubbed dependency is the SUT or a legitimate external boundary; whether a catch-assert is rethrowing; whether a snapshot hunk was reviewed; whether the test exercises framework guarantees. [s22][s19][s10][s15][s11]
One caveat on the AI-agent angle: SpecStory reports "a 2026 study of 86,156 changes to test files by five coding agents found that 80.2% had weak or no explicit oracle signals," while also noting syntax-only checks "can rate a tautological test as strong, because such a test often contains an explicit equality check" — and a hollowtest experiment across 64 agent sessions found the agents did *not* produce hollow tests when writing from a spec, concluding "hollow tests are a human habit first." Both are single-source claims; treat the rates as directional. [s22][s7]
